hints: Look at the three long fatty acid tails in a triglyceride and ask yourself, can water mix with oil?
Remember why lipids release more energy than carbohydrates in respiration, it is all about how much hydrogen versus oxygen they contain.
walkthrough:
**Are triglycerides polar?**

Think of oil and water. They do not mix because triglycerides are non-polar and hydrophobic.

The long hydrocarbon fatty acid tails have no overall charge, so water is repelled. That means polar = no (X).

**Are triglycerides less dense than water?**

Think of oil floating on top of water in cooking or in a spill.

Triglycerides float because they are less dense than water. That means less dense than water = yes (check).

**Do they have less hydrogen than carbohydrates?**

This is the trickiest one. Carbohydrates have a lot of oxygen already (about one O for every C).

Triglycerides have very little oxygen and lots of C-H bonds, so they actually have a HIGHER proportion of hydrogen. That means lower proportion of hydrogen = no (X).

**Match to the table**

We need: polar = X, less dense than water = check, lower hydrogen = X.

That pattern is exactly row C. Well done!

options.A: Says polar = yes, but triglycerides are non-polar and hydrophobic, so this row is wrong.
options.B: Says polar = yes and less dense = no, but triglycerides are non-polar and do float on water, so both are wrong.
options.C: Correctly says non-polar (X), less dense than water (check), and NOT lower in hydrogen (X) because lipids are hydrogen-rich.
options.D: Says less dense = no and lower hydrogen = yes, but oil floats and lipids have more hydrogen than carbohydrates, so both are wrong.
